title: Loan Officer Business Plan for 2027: A December Guide
description: Build a loan officer business plan for 2027: review your 2026 sources, set goals by activity, pick focus partners, and plan for a purchase-driven market.
keywords: purchase business plan for loan officers
image_alt: An open monthly planner lying on a wooden desk

faq.q: When should a loan officer write a business plan?
faq.a: December is ideal. Pipelines are usually lighter, the year's results are nearly complete, and you can start January with a weekly plan already in your calendar instead of building one while files are busy.

faq.q: How do I set realistic loan officer goals?
faq.a: Start with closed loans for the year, then work backward using your own pull-through and conversion rates to find the applications, conversations, and weekly activities you need. Use your real history rather than guesses.

faq.q: What does a purchase-driven market mean for my plan?
faq.a: With industry forecasts pointing to flat purchase volume and lower refinance volume in 2027, more of your business will likely come from agent, past-client, and partner relationships, so your plan should invest time there first.

body_html:
Every December I watch the same thing happen. Pipelines thin out, holiday parties fill the calendar, and a lot of loan officers decide they'll "figure out next year in January." Then January arrives, the phones pick up, and the plan never gets written. By March they're reacting to whatever lands in their inbox instead of running the business they wanted to build.

The loan officers I've seen grow year after year treat December as planning season. They don't wait for a perfect market. They look honestly at the year they just had, decide what next year should look like, and turn that into a weekly rhythm they can actually keep. Here's the simple framework I use with my team to build a loan officer business plan for 2027.

Start with the market you'll actually be working in

A plan built on hope falls apart by February. A plan built on a realistic read of the market holds up. The Mortgage Bankers Association's latest outlook, released at its annual convention in October, points to a purchase-driven year. As National Mortgage Professional reported, MBA expects total single-family originations to dip about 5% in 2027 to just under $2 trillion, with purchase volume roughly flat at about $1.42 trillion and refinance volume down about 17%. Mortgage Professional's coverage of the same forecast puts refinance volume near $571 billion.

Fannie Mae's economists see a similar picture. Their October outlook, covered by HousingWire, projects purchase originations essentially flat in 2027 while cutting their refinance estimate sharply.

Forecasts change, and nobody should bet a career on one. But the direction is clear enough to plan around: next year's business will mostly come from people buying homes, which means it will mostly come from relationships. If your 2026 depended on refinances, your 2027 plan needs to look different.

Review 2026 honestly, by source

Before you set a single goal, pull every loan you closed this year and every application that didn't close. Then sort them by where they came from. Most loan officers are surprised by what they find.

  • Agent referrals: Which agents sent you deals, and how many each? Usually a small handful account for most of it.
  • Past clients and their referrals: How many came back or sent a friend?
  • Your personal sphere: Friends, family, community, social media.
  • Other partners: Financial planners, CPAs, builders, attorneys.
  • Applications that fell out: Why? Credit, income documentation, appraisal, buyer cold feet, or slow follow-up on your side?

Be just as honest about where your time went. If you spent hours every week on a channel that produced nothing, that's the first thing to cut. If two agents produced most of your purchase business with very little marketing effort, that's the first thing to double down on.

Work backward from goals to weekly activity

Here's where most plans go wrong. People write a big annual number at the top of a page and stop there. A goal you can't break into this week's activity isn't a plan. It's a wish.

I have my team set goals in units, not dollars, and then work backward using their own numbers from the review above:

  1. Closed loans for the year. Pick a number that stretches you but that you believe.
  2. Applications needed. Use your real pull-through rate from 2026. If roughly half your applications closed, you need about twice as many applications as closings.
  3. Conversations needed. How many meaningful conversations with buyers turned into an application? Again, use your history, not a guess.
  4. Weekly activity. Divide by about 48 working weeks. Now you know how many agent meetings, past-client calls, and buyer consultations each week requires.

That last number is the one that matters. You can't control whether a buyer wins a bidding war. You can control whether you made your calls on Tuesday morning.

Choose your focus partners and your niche

Trying to be everything to every agent in Southern California is a fast way to be forgettable. A stronger plan picks a short list of agents to invest in deeply and a type of borrower you want to be known for serving well.

For partners, I'd rather see a loan officer build ten strong agent relationships than chase a hundred casual ones. Use your review to pick the agents who already trust you, then add a few you want to earn. Plan what you'll bring them each quarter: market updates, help with tough files, education for their buyers. If you need a refresher on how to earn those relationships, I wrote about building a realtor referral network that lasts.

For a niche, think about who in Orange County and the surrounding markets needs more expertise than a standard file. Self-employed borrowers, veterans, first-time buyers who need help with down payment assistance programs, investors buying rentals. Being the go-to person for one group makes referrals easier, because agents know exactly when to call you.

Build the plan into your calendar

A business plan that lives in a document gets ignored. A plan that lives in your calendar gets done. Once you know your weekly activity numbers, block time for them before anything else fills the week.

Time blockWhat goes in itWhy it matters
Prospecting hour (daily)Agent calls, past-client check-ins, partner follow-upsKeeps the pipeline full when files get busy
Partner meetings (weekly)Coffee, office visits, joint planning with focus agentsTurns contacts into referral relationships
Learning block (weekly)Guidelines, new programs, compliance updatesMakes you the expert people trust with harder files
Pipeline review (weekly)Every active file, every condition, every deadlineProtects closings and your reputation
Quarterly check-inCompare activity and results to the planLets you adjust early instead of in December

Protect the prospecting hour most of all. It's the first thing to disappear when files get busy, and it's the reason so many loan officers swing between feast and famine. I go deeper on that cycle in how top loan officers stay productive in any rate environment.

And while you're planning, put the administrative deadlines in the calendar too: license renewal, continuing education, and your company's marketing review process. They're easy to forget until they're urgent.

The takeaway

You don't need a fancy template to plan a strong 2027. You need an honest look back, a realistic read of a purchase-driven market, goals broken into weekly activity, a focused group of partners, and a calendar that protects the work that matters. Spend a few quiet hours on it this December, and you'll walk into January already knowing what to do on Monday morning.
